verdict.difficultyReason: Our estimate: Sensitive scopes need a manual review. Sources do not settle every factor, so it could be anywhere from moderate to hard.
verdict.useCase: An AI agent that runs as a bot in customers' Discord servers (OAuth2 bot scope) and reads and posts messages. Reading message content needs the Message Content privileged intent.

timeToCredentials.basis: Our estimate: app creation needs only a Discord account and the Developer Portal, with no review before the bot can be added, so it likely takes under a few hours.

timeToProduction.basis: Our estimate: no source gives a review time. Review only applies at 10,000+ users or at annual renewal. A manual review of this kind likely takes weeks, so the range is wide.

humanEffortHours.basis: Our estimate: a few hours to register the app and configure the bot, plus time to draft use case and data-practice answers if the review is triggered. No source gives a figure.

verdict.summary: Registering a Discord app and adding a bot with the Message Content intent is self-serve under 10,000 users. Past that threshold you must apply for the intent, and the sources give no review time or depth.
verdict.biggestLaunchRisk: Once the bot reaches 10,000 unique users, you have 90 days to apply for Message Content access or it is removed. The sources give no review turnaround, and access must be renewed every year.

youNeedOwnWhen.text: Your bot passes 10,000 unique users and needs Privileged Intent access. The application is made in the Developer Portal for the specific app, so you likely need your own app to hold that access.
You want to verify the bot. Verification is tied to a Developer Team owner's ID, and ownership cannot be transferred afterwards.
You want your own app identity, use case documentation and annual renewal under your control. The sources do not say whether a shared app can do this.

requirements.text: A Discord account is needed to register an application in the Developer Portal and get a client ID and client secret.
Message Content is a Privileged Intent. It is disabled by default and gives access to the content, embeds, attachments, components and poll fields of messages.
At 10,000+ unique users, use case documentation is required. The form asks for current app functionality, the use case for each requested intent, and data practices.
Apps that already hold Privileged Intent access must reapply once a year.
To verify the bot, a Developer Team owner aged 16 or over must submit a qualifying ID through Stripe. This is a personal ID, and the sources do not mention a business entity being required.
The Developer Policy requires explicit permission before changing a user's account or starting processes on a user's or server's behalf.

steps.title: Sign in with a Discord account
steps.detail: You need a Discord account to register a developer application. Any verification prompts Discord shows for the account are not described in the sources.

steps.title: Read the OAuth2 and Developer Policy docs
steps.detail: Review the OAuth2 flows, the bot scope, and the policy on user permission and server permission. Note that some scopes need Discord approval.

steps.title: Register the application and save credentials
steps.detail: Create the application in the Developer Portal and retrieve the client ID and client secret. A community report says one OAuth failure came from using the public key instead of the application secret.
steps.agentPrep: Prepare a secrets-storage plan and a checklist that distinguishes the public key from the client secret.

steps.title: Configure the bot scope and invite link
steps.detail: Use the bot scope so the bot is added to the guild the installer selects. The applications.commands scope is included by default with it.

steps.title: Enable the Message Content intent in the Developer Portal
steps.detail: On the app's Bot page, under Privileged Gateway Intents, toggle on Message Content. This works without applying while the app has under 10,000 unique users. Enable only what the bot actually needs.

steps.title: Build the bot to read and post messages
steps.estimate: Depends on scope of the agent
steps.detail: Without the intent, the app cannot access message content fields. Make sure server owners clearly consent to the bot acting in their servers.

steps.title: Watch the unique-user count and prepare use case documentation
steps.detail: At 10,000 unique users the app or team owner is notified by email or system DM, and the Developer Portal shows a message. Draft answers on app functionality, the Message Content use case, and data practices.
steps.agentPrep: Draft the Message Content justification, a description of current functionality, and a data practices summary.

steps.title: Submit the Privileged Intent application within 90 days
steps.detail: Submit through the Developer Portal within 90 days of the notification. If you miss the window, intent access is removed, though you can still apply later.

steps.title: Wait for Discord's review decision
steps.detail: The app keeps working with the requested intents and can keep joining servers during review. No source states the review duration or whether it is manual.

steps.title: Reapply each year to keep access
steps.detail: After the annual notification you have 90 days to reapply. Keep your use case documentation current.
steps.agentPrep: Keep a refreshed copy of the use case and data practices text ready.

steps.title: Optional: verify the bot with a qualifying ID
steps.detail: A Developer Team owner aged 16 or over submits a qualifying ID to Stripe from the Developer Portal. After approval, the team fills out and submits the verification application. The sources do not say whether verification is required for this use case.
steps.agentPrep: Move the app to a Developer Team and make sure the team owner has a qualifying ID ready.

scopesAndNuances.text: The bot scope puts the bot in the selected guild. Some OAuth2 scopes need Discord approval, and requesting them without approval may cause errors or undocumented behavior.
The three Privileged Intents are Guild Presences, Guild Members and Message Content. Your use case needs Message Content only, so do not request the others unless needed.

As of June 10, 2026, the review threshold is based on unique users who can see the app across all its servers, not server count. A bot in a few large servers can hit the threshold sooner than a bot in many small ones.
Token and revocation endpoints accept only application/x-www-form-urlencoded, not JSON.
Scopes such as applications.builds.upload are for approved partners only, via a Discord account representative. They are not needed for this use case.
A community report says the Developer Portal's display of public key and secret is confusing. A real secret is short and alphanumeric, not the long hash-like key.
The provider's published OAuth metadata lists: PKCE: S256; no registration endpoint is listed.

blockers.problem: The 90-day window to apply after the 10,000-user notification passes without an application.
blockers.fix: Submit the Privileged Intent application in the Developer Portal. You can apply again at any time to request access back.

blockers.problem: The bot cannot see message content.
blockers.fix: Check that Message Content is toggled on in the Bot page or approved for the app. Without it, the app has no access to those fields.

blockers.problem: The intended verifying team owner is under 16 or has no qualifying ID.
blockers.fix: Add a Developer Team owner aged 16 or over with a qualifying ID, such as a co-developer, parent or guardian. They must apply from their own account, and ownership cannot be transferred after verification.
Check that you are using the application secret, not the public key. Reset the secret under your app's OAuth2 page if needed.
